items.content_html:

An exceptionally strong 2026–27 El Niño is disrupting food production and prompting emergency measures. Peru declared an emergency across more than 70% of its municipalities over flood danger, with authorities warning that more than 9 million people face a high risk of floods and landslides. In the Philippines, unmilled rice production fell 18% in the three months to September, while forecasters expect below-normal rainfall in November. Nearly 896,000 hectares have burned in Indonesia since January; smoke has led to school closures and respiratory illness, according to a report citing BBC. Cereal maker Kellanova has also changed the ingredients in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops sold in the UK and Europe, citing weather-related problems with the availability and quality of rice and grains. The UN’s International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) says overlapping climate and economic shocks could cost the global economy as much as $11 trillion, with energy and fertilizer costs adding pressure across food systems. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said in September it had received only one-fifth of the $202 million requested to prepare for food crises in 22 high-risk countries.

The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. items.title: [news.un.org] UN warns 2026 heat records signal accelerating climate extremes
items.content_html: Earth’s energy imbalance has reached its highest level since monitoring began, and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Global surface temperature averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level from January through September; a developing, unusually strong El Niño could push the annual figure higher and prolong extreme heat into 2027. The agency released its report as the U.N. climate summit COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiations scheduled through Nov. 20. The agency says each of the past 12 years ranked among the 12 warmest on record, with 2023-2026 likely to be the four warmest years. Greenhouse gases from human activity are trapping heat; the ocean absorbs about 90% of the excess, while sea levels and ocean temperatures have reached records. The WMO warns that the accumulating heat will intensify heat waves, droughts, tropical cyclones and heavy rain. A separate U.N. Environment Programme assessment says warming will exceed 1.5°C under every plausible emissions pathway. Returning below that threshold this century would require near-zero emissions and the removal of hundreds of billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide. The WMO’s full 2026 climate report is due in March 2027.

items.title: [euronews.com] Early Arctic vortex disruption raises cold risk; climate link remains unproven
items.content_html: Meteorologists are tracking an unusually early weakening of the Arctic polar vortex, a circulation high above the pole. Its disruption can shift atmospheric patterns and increase the chance of cold outbreaks across parts of Europe, North America and Asia. The event is occurring in early November, weeks or months before major disruptions usually develop. Its effects may take weeks to reach weather systems near the surface. Climate change has been suggested as a possible influence on the atmospheric processes involved, but researchers have not established a direct link to this event, and the proposed connection remains disputed. Scientists are also assessing the influence of a strong El Niño and natural variability. The weather effects depend on how the disturbance develops and interacts with other atmospheric systems.

items.title: [scimex.org] Heatwave feedback can add 10% to extreme temperatures, study finds
items.content_html: A study led by Yinglin Tian, a scientist at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, found that interactions among heat, dry soils and high atmospheric pressure can make the most extreme mid-latitude heatwaves about 10% hotter. High pressure brings more sunlight to the surface, while dry soils provide less evaporative cooling. In Central Europe, the threshold for this feedback is about 29°C; the chance of crossing it rose from 6% in 1979–83 to 23% in 2018–22. The researchers used machine learning and statistical analysis to identify the process, which they say current heat forecasting models do not represent well. A separate study led by Freie Universität Berlin researcher Philipp Aglas-Leitner compared 22 exceptional heatwaves from 2010–23 with projections through 2100. It found that future events could last longer and affect larger areas. For many regions, most model ensembles project at least one exceptional heatwave period a year in 2060–99.

The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. The Korea Meteorological Administration said temperatures in November, December and January are likely to exceed long-term averages, with more rain than usual in November and December. It also warned that cold spells remain possible. The agency said the average sea-surface temperature in the Pacific monitoring region from August through October was 2.4°C above normal, the highest for that period since records began in 1950. The event may also affect global annual temperatures, but forecasts differ: Berkeley Earth puts the chance that 2026 will be the warmest year on record at 96%, while the U.S. National Centers for Environmental Information puts it at 0.1% and gives the year an 86.9% chance of ranking second. Scientists say El Niño’s warming influence comes from heat accumulated in the ocean, much of it linked to greenhouse-gas emissions. Its largest effect on global temperatures is expected in 2027. Recent storms in the Southwest killed at least four people, and Clovis, New Mexico, recorded 28.84 inches of rain since Sept. 20, compared with a historical average of 3.3 inches.

items.title: [rte.ie] COP31 set to open in Türkiye with fossil-fuel and finance disputes
items.content_html: Nearly 200 countries are due to begin the U.N. COP31 climate talks in Antalya on Nov. 9, with negotiations scheduled to run through Nov. 20 and more than 100,000 participants expected. Türkiye will host while Australia leads negotiations under a compromise over the summit’s location. The conference will focus on implementing earlier climate pledges rather than agreeing on new targets. The agenda includes Türkiye’s push to raise electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035, preferably using renewable power, and efforts to include electrification in the summit’s final political statement. Disputes are expected over stronger language on phasing out fossil fuels and whether wealthy countries will provide more funding for developing nations adapting to climate impacts. Türkiye’s environment minister and COP31 president, Murat Kurum, says the summit should turn previous commitments into results. The European Union wants electrification explicitly described as “clean,” while African negotiators are pressing to add a pledge to triple adaptation finance to the agenda. The Trump administration will not take part in the negotiations, although a U.S. congressional delegation is expected to attend.
